title: Sitting down on the shore
hookLine: late, empty-handed, and tempted to hide or give up

cards: On the beach, Angada does the math, and it's bad. They're late. They haven't found Sita.
Sugriva warned that anyone who came back late would answer with their life. And Angada carries a private fear on top of that. He's Vali's son.
His uncle took his father's throne with Rama's help. Angada wonders whether Sugriva has ever really trusted him. Back late and empty-handed?
He decides he isn't going back at all.

teach.b: Despair spreads fast. Angada tells the others he'll fast to death right here on the shore, a vow called prayopavesha.
One monkey, named Tara, a different Tara from Vali's widow, offers another way out: let's go back to the cave. It has food, water, safety, and no one could reach us. Several monkeys like the idea.
Then Hanuman speaks. To Angada he's gentle: Sugriva is fair, and you're dear to him; don't assume the worst. About the cave he's blunt: Lakshmana's arrows could split that cave open.
Hiding isn't safety. And quietly he wins the others over, one by one. Angada isn't convinced.

He spreads sacred darbha grass on the shore and sits down, and the others sit with him, a long line along the sea, talking about Rama and Sita, and about Jatayu, the old vulture who died fighting Ravana.
The Bhagavad Gita opens with it: the warrior Arjuna, facing a duty he can't bear, drops his bow and sinks down in his chariot. Krishna's first answer, more or less, is: stand up.
The teaching under both scenes is dharma, your rightful duty, the part that's yours to do. Being late doesn't cancel it. Being afraid doesn't cancel it.
Despair says sit down and disappear; dharma says go back, tell the truth, and keep going. And up on the hillside behind them, out of a cave, something very old is listening.

how: Prayopavesha, fasting unto death, appears in the epics as a solemn vow; Hindu teachers today speak of it only in very specific traditional contexts, and in the Ramayana the monkeys' vow is interrupted before it's carried out.

o: a prayer for safe passage across the sea
a fast kept for one day before a holy rite
sitting down to fast unto death, a solemn vow

games.q: on the shore — tap the pairs.
p: sits down to fast to death
spread on the shore for the vow

s: the Gita opens with Arjuna sitting down in despair, too
he drops his bow in his chariot, and Krishna tells him to stand up.
Hanuman says hiding in the cave isn't safe
Lakshmana's arrows could split it open.
Angada sits down to fast anyway, and the others join him.

games.q: you're Hanuman. your leader wants to fast to death, and others want to hide in the cave. what do you do?
o: join the fast out of loyalty.
argue against both: Sugriva is fair, and hiding isn't safe.
games.why: Hanuman argues against both: going back is still their duty, their dharma. Angada sits down to fast anyway.

practice: Notice, gently, whether there's somewhere in your life you've quietly sat down and given up, not to fix it now, just to see it.

Breathe in and name it; breathe out and ask what your part there still is, one small next step: a call, an apology, showing up late instead of never. If you pray, many Hindus call on Hanuman when they're afraid; you can too.
If giving up ever feels like more than that, please reach out today: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

wordCard.voice: Prayopavesha, sitting down to fast unto death: the vow Angada takes today on the shore, when Hanuman argues that hiding in the cave isn't safety either.

orig.note: Sanskrit prāyopaveśa: sitting down to fast unto death, a solemn vow in the epics.

carryVoice: Your line: despair doesn't cancel your dharma. Even here, the story isn't over. See you tomorrow.
